body_markdown:
Hot Wheels has created over 25,000 different models, but leave it to a bunch of car people to choose examples that fall outside of that portfolio. When we put the question to our staff—which vehicle would you like to see immortalized as a 1:64-scale model—they were not slow in identifying meaningful models from their past, or other fascinating examples based on their tastes. With the exception of Sajeev’s flamboyant prewar selection, this is a rather humble grouping of vintage cars that would nevertheless delight us if parked on our desks in miniature form.


Read our rationale behind our five choices, and then tell us which classics you’d submit for[Hot Wheels’](https://www.hagerty.com/media/video/geek-out-for-61-minutes-with-a-real-life-hot-wheels-designer/) (or Matchbox’s or Green Light or Auto World’s) consideration below!


## Delage D8 120 Coupe


Broad Arrow


I knew there are a lot of cars that Hot Wheels has already immortalized, but I was a little surprised that the 1938 Phantom Corsair already made it into this coveted space. But I have yet to see a Delage D8 120 Coupe, and that’s a shame! French cars of the Art Deco era are so stunning to behold, as witnessed by the Hot Wheels Talbot Lago. So give us a Delage, Hot Wheels! Pretty please? — *Sajeev Mehta*


## Chevrolet Special Deluxe Convertible


Eddy Eckart


My Grandpa Ed’s 1941—I think—Chevy Special Deluxe Convertible. This question was a good exercise, because when I considered my response, I checked and there are, in fact, die-casts of this Chevy out there. I’m keeping my answer, though, and am going to buy one tonight! The above photo is the oldest image I have of someone in my family with a car. A couple years home from the war, Gramp, who was a Pearl Harbor survivor, worked in Washington, D.C., but his heart was with Mary Luzar in Cleveland, Ohio, where they both grew up. I imagine him hustling this convertible on what must’ve been a long journey to see his sweetheart—my grandma—on his time off. They’re both gone now, but I love this photo and imagine what a fancy ride it must have been for someone who had just come back from the war. *— Eddy Eckart*


## Cooper S Mini


Andrew Newton


Andrew Newton


To also go the sentimental route, I have a painting of my dad’s 1971 Cooper S Mini (no idea where it came from). I also have a classic Mini Hot Wheels car—okay, I have three of them. I have a few memories of the car itself, but it would be great to have an exact lil’ copy of the real thing, details and all, to have on my desk. *— Andrew Newton*


## Willys Jeep Station Wagon


Flickr / Alden Jewell


I’ll choose the car that introduced me to old cars: A 1950s Willys Jeep station wagon. Okay, so it’s a truck, that is called a station wagon … anyways, it belonged to my great-grandfather and was in my dad’s stewardship when I encountered it, probably around the age of five or six. “The Jeep” was painted red and white, and I remember none of the facts and figures I’d want to know today, like model year and engine displacement. What I remember are details like the pointy W on the horn button, the whiny churn of the transmission, the pale plastic knob on the handle for the roll-up windows, the long, skinny gas pedal, and what seemed like an excessive number of stalks protruding from the floor. (Seriously, wasn’t one shifter enough?) Hot Wheels has created many Willys models, with appropriate attention given to hot rods and[gassers](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/this-longtime-willys-fan-drives-the-gasser-of-his-dreams/) , but I’d love to own a plain-jane model of this humble old truck. *— Grace Jarvis*


## Subaru Justy … But Wait, There’s More


Subaru


Matchbox has a real opportunity here to launch a Sh%tbox Collection with all the small, efficient, detestable stuff of yore that no one *really* liked but everybody recognized as necessary. Your Datsun 210s and VW Foxes and[Hyundai Excels](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/if-early-hyundais-ever-become-collectible-these-will-be-the-cars-to-have/) . I’d ask them to start with the Subaru Justy—one FWD and one 4WD, just to cover all bases. They could probably fit one of each of the little 3-cylinder runabouts into a single blister back. I’d happily pay $2 for that. *— Stefan Lombard*
